title: The numinous
hook: Rudolf Otto named the holy as a mystery that makes us tremble and draws us in (The Idea of the Holy)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Carl Sagan. Your line was the cosmos has a way to know itself. Where did that line find you? Today a scholar of religion tries to name the feeling underneath all this awe. Day one thousand twenty-seven.
screen: `THE COSMOS HAS A WAY TO KNOW ITSELF.`

segments.voice: A storm rolls in after dark. The power cuts out. Lightning shows the whole street for half a second, then nothing. Some people pull the curtains shut. Others drift to the window, a little scared, and can't stop looking. Back away, come closer, both in the same body at the same moment. Rudolf Otto, a scholar of religion, wrote a whole book about that double pull. He thought it sat near the heart of what people mean when they call something holy. And he decided the old words weren't good enough for it. He needed a new one.
screen: `THE STORM AT THE WINDOW.` → `BACK AWAY, COME CLOSER.` → `A NEW WORD FOR THE HOLY.`

segments.voice: Otto's book is called The Idea of the Holy. First, his complaint. When people say holy, he noticed, they often just mean perfectly good. Otto thought that leaves something out: something stranger than goodness, a sense of a presence that is wholly other. He wanted a word for that part alone, so he made one. From the Latin numen, a word for divine power or presence, he formed numinous. Second, he said the numinous can't be strictly defined. It can only be pointed at until the listener recognizes it, the way you'd help someone recognize a smell. So he gave it a Latin description: mysterium tremendum et fascinans. Mysterium: a mystery, beyond our grasp. Tremendum: something to tremble before, so overwhelming it makes a person feel small. He called that creature-feeling. Third, the half that's easy to miss: fascinans. Fascinating. Drawing you in. For Otto the holy doesn't only frighten. It attracts. The trembling and the drawing near arrive together. Fourth, an old scene that holds both halves. In the book of Exodus, Moses sees a bush burning that doesn't burn up, and in the King James words he says, "I will now turn aside, and see this great sight." He walks toward it. A moment later, "Moses hid his face; for he was afraid to look upon God." Toward, and away. Otto was a Christian theologian, and readers argue about his theology. But the word he made has traveled far beyond his book. A storm, a birth, the sea at night, a silence in a very old room: some moments ask for a bigger word than nice. Numinous is one.
screen: `HOLY MEANS MORE THAN GOOD.` · `POINTED AT, NOT DEFINED.` · `TREMENDUM AND FASCINANS.` · `MOSES TURNS ASIDE, THEN HIDES.` · then, large: `MYSTERIUM TREMENDUM ET FASCINANS.`

segments.voice: Settle, and let the breath slow. Bring back one moment that made you tremble: not danger alone, but something too big. A storm. A newborn. The ocean after dark. A piece of music. A silence in an old building. Stay inside that moment. Was there a part of you that wanted to step back? Was there a part that wanted to step closer? Let both be there, if they were. Don't explain the moment. Just stand in it again. If you pray, you can bring it into your prayer. The bell holds the time.
Numinous. Rudolf Otto's word for the holy as a mystery that makes us tremble and draws us in. Today's word.
Your line: tremble and draw near. Today, when something stops you, a sky, a sound, a face, don't hurry past it. Take one step closer. Day one thousand twenty-seven.

howItsDone: Students of religion use Rudolf Otto's word numinous for the sense of a holy presence that is both overwhelming and attractive; some people who practice no religion use it for moments in nature or music that feel too large for ordinary words.

original.note: Latin: divine power or presence. Otto formed the word numinous from it.
